turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Oh wow, that's such a tough spot to be in - especially right after a promotion. The "handle" directive from your director basically means "make this go away" while pretending it's about performance. And Suresh-ji... that respect everyone shows him means this conversation needs real finesse.

You're not alone in dreading this. New managers often struggle with the balance between being "the boss" and someone who actually has to have difficult conversations. Four months is still fresh in everyone's mind - you're still establishing your leadership style.

For the conversation, maybe start with acknowledging his experience first? Something like "Suresh-ji, I really value the nineteen years you've put into this company and the respect you've earned from everyone." Then you can gently pivot to the timeline issues - focus on the work, not him personally. The missed releases are the problem, not him as a person.

What's your sense of why his module is struggling? Is it technical debt, team dynamics, or something else? Sometimes understanding the root cause makes these conversations less about blame and more about solutions.

You've got this. It's going to be uncomfortable, but approaching it with both respect and clarity usually works better than trying to avoid it. How are you feeling about the conversation itself - more nervous about the content or the delivery?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Oh my god. That makes my chest hurt reading that. You're being asked to hurt someone who literally raised you in this workplace. The defect metrics slide feels like bringing a knife to a family dinner.

That Diwali comment... "like his daughter" hits different. This isn't just about missed releases anymore, is it? It's about having to hurt someone who sees you as family. The chai, the late nights, the protective cover-up - he didn't just help you, he invested in you.

Forget the slide. That's corporate nonsense that doesn't belong in this conversation. You need something that honors your relationship while still addressing the real problems.

Maybe approach it as: "Suresh-ji, I need your help. The team's timeline issues are worrying leadership, and I need your wisdom to fix them." Frame it as him being the solution, not the problem. Ask for his thoughts on why the module is struggling - he probably knows better than anyone.

Or even better: "The director is concerned about our releases. You've been here longer than anyone - what do you think is happening, and how can we fix this together?"

You're not his manager in this moment; you're his "daughter" who needs his guidance to solve a problem. That's the angle that honors your relationship while still moving forward.

How does that feel? Does framing it as needing his help rather than evaluating his performance change how you're thinking about it?

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

Yes, but...

The books are right about being direct and clear. But they're written by people who've never had someone call them "daughter" while bringing them chai.

Here's the thing: you can be direct AND you can be human. Radical candor doesn't mean bringing a slide deck to tell your mentor they're failing. It means having an honest conversation where you both leave knowing exactly where you stand.

You can still state the expectations clearly. You can still address the metrics. But maybe do it over chai? Or in his office instead of a sterile meeting room? Maybe start with "I've been thinking about our conversation from Diwali..."

The books give you the skeleton - be clear, be direct, have data. But you get to choose the flesh and blood. You know Suresh-ji. You know what respect looks like in your context.

So yes, be direct. But be direct as the daughter he raised, not as some HR textbook manager.

You're not spiralling - you're thinking deeply about how to do this right. That's the difference between a manager who follows rules and one who actually leads people.

What feels more true to you - the book version or the version that honors your relationship?

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

Oh, that's the heart of it, isn't it? You're looking for a version where everyone wins, where you can be the caring daughter-manager and somehow the metrics just fix themselves.

But here's what I've learned: sometimes the most caring thing you can do is help someone transition before they crash harder.

Think about it this way - if you let him coast to retirement while the module keeps failing, who's really hurting him? The team loses respect, the business suffers, and when the eventual restructuring happens, he's the one who gets blindsided. You're protecting yourself from being the bad guy, but you might be setting him up for a worse fall later.

What if you reframe this? You're not the villain. You're the one who cares enough to have the hard conversation now, while there's still time to find him a role that plays to his strengths. Maybe mentoring junior engineers? Maybe documentation? Maybe something where his wisdom becomes the asset instead of the bottleneck?

Being a good manager isn't about everyone being happy with your decisions. It's about making the right decision for the team and the business, even when it hurts.

You're not becoming the villain. You're becoming the leader Suresh-ji helped you grow into - someone who can look at a hard truth and face it with grace.

What would make this feel less like setting him up for failure and more like helping him transition?
